Werner has spent years building its answer. The company has a long record of hiring veterans and has repeatedly been recognized as a top military-friendly employer. We spoke with Greg Hamm, Vice President of Government and Field Recruiting at Werner, about how that effort works today, why team driving has become a central piece of it and what a veteran can expect from the first day of orientation to a permanent truck.
A pipeline, not a campaign
Plenty of carriers run a Veterans Day promotion and call it a military strategy. Hamm said Werner’s approach is built differently.
“Werner approaches military recruitment not as a promotional campaign, but as a core talent pipeline embedded across operations,” Hamm said.
The numbers support that. Approximately 15% of Werner’s workforce are veterans, military spouses or currently serving. The company also keeps a dedicated military recruiting team made up entirely of veterans, people who understand the nuances of military-to-civilian transitions because they have made that transition themselves.
Team driving sits inside that strategy by design. “Team driving serves as a natural bridge within that strategy,” Hamm said. The logic comes from how service members already work. “Service members are accustomed to operational partnerships, shared accountability and working under tight schedules,” he said.
Werner recruits veteran team pairings in several forms: two veterans who served together, a veteran paired with a spouse or relative or solo drivers matched through Werner’s internal Team Matching program. The carrier gives those teams priority on the freight where uptime matters most. “Teams receive high priority on dedicated, expedited and drop-and-hook routes, providing veterans with higher equipment turnaround, strong earning potential and the camaraderie inherent to military units,” Hamm said.
Why the skills transfer
When you ask fleet executives what makes a great driver and the answer usually involve judgment, discipline and comfort with equipment. Hamm said veterans tend to arrive with all three.
“Veterans possess foundational traits that align seamlessly with commercial motor vehicle (CMV) driving,” he said, and he pointed to three in particular.
Safety First . Hamm explained that “the military instills risk assessment protocols and strict adherence to standard operating procedures (SOPs).” In trucking, he said, that matters because managing blind spots, traffic, tight spaces and pre- and post-trip inspections is paramount, so the habit “directly translates to reduced incident rates.”
Heavy equipment is nothing new. “Many military occupational specialties (MOS) involve operating or maintaining heavy tactical vehicles, tracked equipment or complex logistics networks, removing the intimidation factor of operating an 80,000-lb tractor-trailer,” Hamm said.
Remain cool under pressure . For anyone who has run freight through a January storm or a rerouted delivery window, the comparison is easy to draw. “Military personnel are trained to handle uncertain plans, severe weather and dynamic environments without compromising mission objectives,” Hamm said.
Programs that reduce friction
Recruiting veterans takes more than a welcoming message. The transition has a cost, and carriers that ignore it lose candidates to the first employer that doesn’t. Hamm described Werner’s programs as “structured, federally certified pathways designed to minimize friction and maximize earning power during the civilian transition.”
The apprenticeship program is what makes this transition seamless. “Werner launched the industry’s first Registered Truck Driver Apprenticeship,” Hamm said. The program is approved by the Department of Labor and the VA. Eligible veterans can use GI Bill® or VA educational benefits to receive a tax-free monthly housing allowance directly from the VA, on top of their full Werner paycheck, while they complete on-the-job training. “An eligible veteran can earn up to $37,020 tax-free over the course of two years,” Hamm said.
For service members who have already operated heavy equipment in uniform, there are two other routes. Those who did so within two years of leaving military service, can have their platoon commander sign the Military Skills Test Waiver and submit it to their DMV, which waives the road test. The Even Exchange Program waives the knowledge test in participating states. Werner then recognizes that experience once the driver is hired. “For drivers who obtain their CDL through either program, Werner credits your military experience upon hire, qualifying you for a higher pay rate and a wider variety of account options,” Hamm said.
Education support extends beyond the cab. Werner offers CDL school tuition reimbursement of up to $15,000, including GI Bill® tuition reimbursement. It also offers education assistance through discounts with various university’s providing up to $2,500 per year.
Recognition and community are part of the package as well. The Operation Freedom Fleet is Werner’s flagship military recognition fleet, featuring custom-wrapped, military-tribute Kenworth, Peterbilt and Freightliner tractors. The trucks are awarded to currently serving or veteran drivers who maintain spotless safety and service records. Selection to drive one honors the driver’s service and includes attendance at military installations, industry expos, corporate events and school outreach events. Internally, the WEVets associate resource group connects military drivers, shop technicians, office associates and military spouses nationwide for mentorship, transition support, community engagement and career development.
Reframing team driving
Team driving is often the harder sell, even to experienced drivers. Hamm said the best way to address that is to walk through what teams get and then take on the common objections.
On earnings, the structure is different from solo driving. “Werner attributes pay directly to the truck rather than just individual wheel time,” Hamm said. Because team trucks can legally run 4,500 to 5,500+ miles per week by rotating duty cycles, both drivers benefit from split mileage rates that consistently outpace solo weekly miles.
Freight and equipment are the second draw. Team units handle expedited, high-priority and coast-to-coast dedicated freight, and Hamm said Werner prioritizes teams for the newest tractors in its fleet, typically under 1.5 to 2 years old, along with predominantly drop-and-hook customer accounts.
Safety is the third. “Having a co-driver provides a built-in spotter during tight backing maneuvers, a secondary navigator in complex urban corridors and companionship that helps combat highway fatigue,” Hamm said.
Hamm also addressed three misconceptions he hears often.
Teams never get any rest while the truck is rolling. Hamm said modern tractors have changed that. They are engineered with advanced cab suspension systems, custom premium sleeper mattresses and noise-dampening insulation to ensure the off-duty driver gets restorative rest.
A driver must already have a partner . Many teams are husband-and-wife or military buddies, but that isn’t a requirement. “Werner’s structured Team Matching program pairs drivers based on personality, smoking preferences, route interests and geographic home-time hubs,” Hamm said.
Team drivers give up all personal space . Hamm said the reality is more orderly. “Team drivers establish clear shift boundaries, communication norms, and route splits, creating an efficient and predictable work rhythm,” he said. For veterans used to defined roles and clear communication, that structure should feel familiar.
What onboarding looks like
A driver’s first few weeks usually decide whether they stay. Hamm said Werner’s process “accommodates varying levels of prior experience,” and it starts the same way for everyone. Orientation runs two to three days at a Werner terminal. Drivers complete DOT physical screenings, road evaluations, regulatory compliance briefings and instruction on Werner’s proprietary cab technology systems and workflow apps.
After orientation, the path depends on background. Drivers who hold a CDL through the Military Skills Test Waiver go through an accelerated finishing phase. It focuses on civilian DOT compliance, electronic logging devices (ELDs), sliding tandems and customer service, not basic vehicle handling. New entrants and CDL school graduates complete a multi-week on-road mentorship under a certified Werner Driver Leader. They earn a set weekly salary while they work on freight handling, winter driving, trip planning, customer communication and backing maneuvers.
Veterans in the Registered Apprenticeship program get extra administrative support. The military recruiting team coordinates the submission of all Werner and VA paperwork, as well as monthly certifications directly to the VA, so drivers don’t have to manage the process themselves. Once mentoring is complete, drivers or teams are assigned their permanent truck and route network, whether Dedicated, 48-state OTR or Regional.
Support beyond the paycheck
Retention depends on what a driver’s life looks like away from the highway, and for veterans with families, that matters a great deal. Hamm said Werner’s operating model includes infrastructure aimed at those needs.
Concerning scheduling, dedicated fleets, used in specific retail accounts, closed-loop manufacturing and expedited parcel freight, offer “predictable routing, pre-scheduled home time and stable weekly pay guarantees,” Hamm said.
Family support is part of the structure too. “Werner extends Career Currency to family members of drivers and mechanics,” he said.
Health coverage includes comprehensive medical, dental and vision after 30 days of active employment, a company-matched 401(k), and on-site medical clinics at major terminal facilities. Werner also offers pet and authorized passenger ride-along programs. “To support mental well-being and flexibility, Werner offers both pet and authorized passenger ride-along programs,” Hamm said. For teams, and for any driver who spends weeks away from home, those policies can make a real difference.
Where this leaves carriers
Werner’s approach points to a broader lesson for fleets weighing how to recruit veterans. The strongest programs treat military experience as a skill set with real operational value, give it credit in pay and account placement, and pair it with a structure that mirrors how service members already work. Team driving, in Hamm’s framing, is one of the places where all of that comes together.
Veterans bring discipline, equipment familiarity and a habit of working as part of a unit. A carrier that builds pathways for those strengths, from apprenticeship to team matching to a dedicated recruiting staff made up of fellow veterans, gives itself a better chance of turning a first job in trucking into a long career.
